name: NZX Limited
overview: NZX Limited operates New Zealand's only registered securities exchange, providing listing, trading, clearing, settlement, depository and data services across equity, debt, funds, derivatives (dairy and equity) and energy markets. Beyond exchange operations, NZX owns Smart (formerly Smartshares), New Zealand's leading passive funds manager and KiwiSaver/ETF provider, and NZX Wealth Technologies (NZXWT), a wealth-administration platform used by financial advisers. NZX is a genuinely small-cap business (~NZ$470m market cap) generating roughly NZ$130-145m of annual revenue, and it is simultaneously the country's front-line market regulator (via NZ RegCo) and a listed company subject to that same regulatory framework.

business_model.summary: Three-segment model: Markets (exchange listing fees, secondary trading/clearing/depository, dairy derivatives, Information Services) is the largest, highest-margin segment (FY2025 EBITDA margin ~64%) but its revenue is flat-to-declining and cyclical; Funds Management (Smart) earns FUM-based fees on ETFs, KiwiSaver and managed funds and has been the fastest-growing segment (+18% revenue FY2025, +19% H1-2026); Wealth Technologies (NZXWT) earns SaaS/platform administration fees from financial advisers based on funds under administration and is growing fastest in percentage terms (+26% H1-2026) off a smaller base. Markets revenue mixes recurring elements (annual listing fees, data/terminal subscriptions) with transactional ones (trading value, capital raised, derivatives lots); Smart and NZXWT revenue is highly recurring, scaling with FUM/FUA balances rather than transaction volume.

revenue_streams.name: Markets (listings, trading/clearing, depository, dairy derivatives, Information Services)
Regulation & Corporate Services (cost recovery, NZ RegCo)

business_model.customer_type: B2B/B2B2C mix: listed issuers, brokers and trading/clearing participants for Markets; retail KiwiSaver and investment-fund members plus wholesale mandates for Smart; independent financial advice firms and institutional wealth managers for NZXWT
business_model.geographic_mix: Almost entirely New Zealand-domiciled revenue and operations; dairy derivatives extend internationally via the Singapore Exchange (SGX) partnership and GlobalDairyTrade auction participants across Asia and the Middle East; Smart and NZXWT are explicitly NZ-focused ('no global distractions')

main_competitors: ASX (Australian Securities Exchange) - the primary competitive threat, via dual/sole listings of NZ companies and NZ-linked equity trading share
Bank- and boutique-owned KiwiSaver/managed-fund providers (Milford Asset Management, Fisher Funds, ANZ Investments, Kiwi Wealth, Simplicity, Booster) competing with Smart/SuperLife
QuayStreet Group - NZX's former active-management subsidiary, externalised in March 2026 into an independent partner that still competes for the same investor wallet
FNZ, Class and other wealth-administration/platform providers competing with NZXWT
Private equity and offshore capital markets as an alternative destination for NZ companies seeking growth capital
Singapore Exchange (SGX) - a dairy-derivatives partner but also a broader competing venue globally
competitive_position.market_position: Sole operator of New Zealand's licensed securities exchange - a legal monopoly on domestic listing/trading infrastructure - but over a genuinely small, low-liquidity market (total market cap ~NZ$244b, roughly 56% of GDP, versus 100%+ in most developed markets per NZX's own disclosure). That monopoly is increasingly disintermediated: ASX's average daily traded value in NZ-linked stocks has already exceeded total NZX cash-market turnover, and ASX's capital pool is roughly four times New Zealand's. Smart is New Zealand's largest passive/ETF manager and a top-tier KiwiSaver-adjacent provider via SuperLife; NZXWT is one of NZ's leading independent wealth-administration platforms but competes against much larger incumbents for adviser mandates.

moat_factors.description: NZX is the only entity licensed to operate a registered securities exchange in New Zealand under the Financial Markets Conduct Act; a rival domestic exchange licence is a high, largely theoretical barrier to entry.

moat_factors.factor: Network effects among listed issuers, brokers and investors
moat_factors.description: Liquidity begets liquidity - the existing issuer base, S&P/NZX index inclusion and broker connectivity create switching costs - but the pool is small enough that network effects are comparatively weak and can run in reverse: delistings reduce liquidity, which then encourages further delistings or ASX migration.

NZX Clearing is the central counterparty for NZ equities, but the parallel RBNZ-owned NZ Clear depository for debt is a dual, inefficient structure that NZX itself is lobbying to consolidate - evidence the current setup is a cost problem, not a clean competitive advantage.

moat_factors.factor: Cross-sell / platform bundling across Markets, Smart and NZXWT
moat_factors.description: Owning the exchange, a funds manager and a wealth-admin platform lets NZX capture fees at multiple points in the KiwiSaver/investment value chain (issuance, trading, fund management, platform administration) - a diversification most single-product NZ competitors lack, and the source of NZX's most credible growth narrative.

160-year incumbency and close government/regulatory relationships support listings origination and policy influence, but brand alone does not compel issuers or capital to remain onshore, as recent delistings show.

weaknesses: Small, structurally illiquid market - NZ's investable capital pool is roughly a quarter the size of Australia's, and ASX's own daily traded value in NZ-linked stocks already exceeds NZX cash-market turnover

No compulsion for NZ issuers to list or remain listed on NZX - dual-listing and outright ASX migration (or going-private) is a well-worn path; NZX's own incoming CEO publicly framed the company as having 'struggled to grow the number of listed companies over the past decade'

Revenue exposed to volatile, cyclical capital-markets activity (new listings, secondary raisings, trading value, IPO pipeline) that management cannot control and that has been persistently soft in 2025-2026

Passive ETF/KiwiSaver fee compression - intense price competition among providers pressures Smart's fee take-rate even as absolute FUM rises, and H1-2026 Smart EBITDA margin (excl. project costs) actually fell year-on-year (45.4% to 42.2%) despite 19% revenue growth, partly reflecting the QuayStreet externalisation cost restructure

Governance duality - NZX is both a for-profit listed company and (via NZ RegCo) the market's frontline regulator, a structural conflict-of-interest optic that persists even with formal governance separation and FMA co-oversight

growth_drivers: KiwiSaver structural tailwind: national KiwiSaver pool was ~NZ$130b at end-2025 and ~NZ$124.5b at March 2026 (up ~10.7% YoY); management estimates the pool could grow more than 5x by 2050. Default contribution rates rise from 3% to 3.5% (April 2026) and to 4% (April 2028), with further increases proposed by some political parties - a direct fee-revenue tailwind for Smart via SuperLife KiwiSaver and Smartshares ETFs

Smart FUM scaling: FUM grew from $2.9b (Dec-2018) to $18.0b (H1-2026), a ~27% CAGR since 2018 (including $3.4b of acquisitions), with management targeting at least $20b by end-2029 and citing $15-20b as the point of peak cost efficiency for an NZ fund manager - implying scope for margin expansion once scale is reached

NZXWT platform scale-up: FUA reached $21.1b (H1-2026, +20% YoY), annual recurring revenue $13.7m (+15% YoY, +26% revenue growth H1-2026); the Craigs Investment Partners custody/private-wealth migration (agreed Dec-2025, live 2027) and the Smart KiwiSaver registry migration (Q4 2026) together open an estimated addressable market of $275b+ for funds registry services and $210b for adviser platforms

S&P/NZX 20 Index Futures re-launch (April 2026) - New Zealand has lacked an active equity derivatives product since 1991; a successful build-out could drive incremental cash-market trading, participation and data revenue, though volumes so far are modest (6,860 lots, $51m notional in H1-2026)

Dairy derivatives partnership with Singapore Exchange (SGX) - lots traded up 22.2% in FY2025 to a record 815,494 (though down 5.7% in H1-2026 against a large prior-year comparator); management sees scope for volumes to reach 1-2x underlying physical volume versus ~0.34x today as speculator/hedger participation matures; GDT's Singapore expansion aims to diversify beyond reliance on Fonterra

Government capital-markets reform agenda - prospective financial information (PFI) made optional for IPOs (June 2025), climate-disclosure thresholds raised, dual-class share structures and tiered SME compliance frameworks under consultation, and 'asset recycling' (partial privatisation/listing of state and council infrastructure assets - ports, airports, lines companies) entering mainstream political discussion
NZX Dark and other market-quality/liquidity initiatives aimed at reversing structural liquidity decline in the cash market

New CEO Hishaam Mirza (ex-NZ Super, 14-year tenure; starts 14 September 2026) has explicitly framed his mandate as building 'greater scale, liquidity and global relevance' - a potential strategic catalyst, though unproven and a genuine execution risk given the CEO transition itself

business.risk: Listing and issuer attrition to ASX or going-private
business.description: Restaurant Brands NZ (delisted Dec-2025), Marsden Maritime (scheme of arrangement, June-2025) and Vital Limited (voluntary delisting, Oct-2025, citing low liquidity) are recent examples; ASX's larger capital pool (~4x NZ's) and deeper liquidity continue to pull growth companies toward sole or dual ASX listings, directly eroding the Markets segment's fee base over time.

business.risk: Weak IPO pipeline and thin primary issuance
business.description: H1-2026 new capital listed fell sharply against a comparative period that was inflated by Fonterra's one-off transfer to the Main Board; management repeatedly cites 'several IPO candidates waiting for less volatile market conditions' - a pipeline that has not converted at scale for several years running.

Total value traded was roughly flat to down in FY2025 and H1-2026 (down 0.9% and 2.7% respectively); low turnover both suppresses trading/clearing fee revenue and is cited by issuers themselves as a reason to migrate liquidity to ASX.

business.risk: Customer/counterparty concentration in dairy derivatives and Information Services
business.description: GlobalDairyTrade profitability depends heavily on Fonterra's take-or-pay arrangement, and dairy derivatives volumes can swing sharply on the presence or absence of a small number of large structured trades.

Growing FUM has not translated one-for-one into EBITDA margin expansion at Smart in the most recent half (margin excl. project costs fell from 45.4% to 42.2% YoY in H1-2026), reflecting both competitive fee pressure and the cost structure change from the QuayStreet externalisation.

financial.description: One-off integration and restructure costs were $1.3m (FY2024), $1.8m (FY2025) and continued at $1.0m in H1-2026 (flat YoY) - relating to QuayStreet integration/externalisation, Smart operational maturation and corporate-function restructuring. These are modest relative to a >$50m EBITDA base but have recurred every period for several years, undermining the 'one-off' characterisation.

Management explicitly flags that NZXWT capitalised platform-development costs will amortise faster as client migrations complete, meaning operating cashflow is expected to grow faster than net profit for a period - a timing risk for anyone using NPAT as the primary earnings proxy.
Net debt was $39.1m at H1-2026 (down from $47.4m a year earlier), modest relative to EBITDA, but net finance expenses (~$3.4m FY2025) are a real drag on an already-thin NPAT base.

regulatory.description: NZX is simultaneously a listed company and, via NZ RegCo, the entity that monitors and enforces market rules for issuers and participants on its own market. Governance separation (independent NZ RegCo board, FMA co-regulation under the FMCA) mitigates but does not eliminate the perception risk, and NZ RegCo does not regulate NZX itself, Smart or NZXWT as related entities - a further structural nuance investors should understand.

NZX's growth thesis leans heavily on favourable government capital-markets reform (PFI relief, disclosure thresholds, KiwiSaver contribution increases, asset recycling) - all subject to political cycles and the 2026 general election; NZX itself notes that the FMA's most recent annual review found no formal recommendations, which is reassuring but underscores how central regulatory relationships are to the investment case.

regulatory.risk: Change in KiwiSaver default settings or provider structure
regulatory.description: Government control over KiwiSaver contribution rates, default provider allocation and scheme structure directly affects Smart's addressable flows; policy could also move in directions that do not favour NZX-owned providers.

macro.risk: NZ economic cycle and business investment
macro.description: Management explicitly links subdued 2025-2026 equity issuance to 'a slower economic cycle, cautious business investment' in New Zealand; a small, single-country revenue base means NZX has no geographic diversification to offset a domestic downturn.

macro.risk: Global market volatility and geopolitical shocks
macro.description: H1-2026 results specifically cite the US-Iran conflict and associated oil-market disruption as depressing primary equity issuance and investor confidence - NZX's Markets segment is a direct pass-through of global risk sentiment despite the domestic focus of its listed base.

Falling NZ short-term interest rates in H2 2025 coincided with a pickup in market activity per management commentary, implying some inverse sensitivity to rates via capital markets activity, though the linkage is indirect.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global exchange operators generally benefit from structural growth in passive investing, data monetisation and post-trade services, but New Zealand's specific market is small, thinly traded and has a weak primary-issuance pipeline; the more durable growth story sits in funds management (KiwiSaver) and wealth-administration technology rather than traditional trading/listing activity
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate to high in the Markets segment (listing fees, secondary capital raised, trading value all track capital-markets sentiment and the NZ economic cycle); low to moderate in Smart and NZXWT, where recurring FUM/FUA-based fees smooth volatility, though fund performance and net flows still move with markets
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Indirect and moderate - falling NZ rates appear correlated with a pickup in capital markets activity (H2 2025 commentary), and net finance expenses on NZX's own modest net debt are a minor direct cost
key_input_costs: Staff remuneration (single largest cost line, ~$48-50m annualised)
Information technology / cloud infrastructure and data feeds
Fund distribution and external investment-manager fees following the QuayStreet externalisation

recent_developments.event: NZX announced the appointment of Hishaam Mirza (ex-NZ Super, 14-year tenure heading direct investments) as permanent Chief Executive, effective 14 September 2026, ending a roughly four-month CEO search following Mark Peterson's retirement. Mirza publicly framed the mandate as building 'greater scale, liquidity and global relevance.'

Mark Peterson (CEO since April 2017) departed following the AGM; Chief Financial and Corporate Officer Graham Law was appointed Acting CEO, with Deputy CFO Amy Trotman as Acting CFO, during the search for a permanent successor.

H1-2026 operating revenue rose 13.3% YoY to $76.6m and normalised EBITDA (ex. project/restructure costs) rose 8.8% to $27.3m; NPAT was $9.8m (+18% YoY). Growth was led by Smart (+19.3% revenue) and NZXWT (+26.1% revenue), while Markets grew a more modest 6.4%. Interim dividend declared at 3.2 cents/share.

S&P/NZX 20 Index Futures successfully re-launched in April 2026 after a multi-year absence of an active NZ equity derivatives product (none since 1991); early volumes are modest (6,860 lots, $51.15m notional, 59.9% on-market activity in the half).

NZX/Smart announced the externalisation of active fund manager QuayStreet Asset Management into an independently owned entity, QuayStreet Group, under a long-term partnership; Smart's fund-expense line rose materially afterward as external manager fees replaced internally incurred costs.
NZXWT and Craigs Investment Partners agreed to extend NZXWT's technology services to Craigs' custody and private-wealth business (live 2027), a significant new addressable-market expansion.
Restaurant Brands New Zealand delisted from the NZX Main Board (final trading day 3 December 2025), continuing a pattern of issuer attrition.
Vital Limited voluntarily delisted, citing low liquidity.
Marsden Maritime Holdings delisted following a scheme of arrangement.

FY2025 annual results: operating revenue $129.0m (+7.3%), normalised EBITDA $53.5m (+11.6%, towards the top of $49.0-54.0m guidance), NPAT $21.5m (+20.2% like-for-like), full-year dividend 6.3 cents/share fully imputed (2024: 6.1 cents). Integration and restructure costs were $1.8m (2024: $1.3m), described as relating to QuayStreet integration, Smart operational maturation and corporate restructuring - not fully one-off given the multi-year recurrence.

Fonterra Co-operative Group's transfer to the NZX Main Board contributed materially to FY2025's headline $21.5b capital listed and raised figure; excluding Fonterra, underlying capital raised still grew 25.2%.

items.metric: Operating earnings (EBITDA) pre project & restructure costs
items.notes: H1-2026 result of $27.3m tracks toward the middle of the range; guidance explicitly subject to market capitalisation, capital listed/raised, value traded, derivatives volumes, FUM/FUA levels, technology/project costs and broader macro conditions, and assumes no material adverse market impacts, one-off expenses, accounting adjustments or M&A.
H1-2026 actual was $6.0b (or $4.8b excluding the Fonterra Main Board transfer), well behind the pace implied by the full-year target, reflecting a subdued primary issuance environment in H1.
H1-2026 actual $21.2b, down 2.7% YoY, roughly on pace for the full-year target but reliant on a stronger H2.
H1-2026 actual 363,800 (down 5.7% YoY against a large prior-year comparator; up 5.3% excluding that comparator).
H1-2026 actual 6,900 lots since the April re-launch; management expects participation to broaden as more brokers and platforms connect.

items.metric: Information Services revenue growth (excl. one-off revenue)
items.notes: H1-2026 actual +7.4% YoY excl. one-off audit/back-dated revenue, ahead of the full-year target pace.
H1-2026 actual FUM growth was 28.5% YoY (to $18.0b), well ahead of the full-year target range, supported by a significant one-off wholesale mandate.
H1-2026 actual already $13.7m, ahead of the full-year target; excludes Craigs Investment Partners ARR, which is due to go live in 2027.

FY2025 normalised free cash flow was ~$66.9m with EBITDA-to-FCF conversion of ~72%; FY2025 total dividend of 6.3 cents/share against NPAT of $21.5m implies a payout close to 100% of statutory NPAT but roughly 80% of normalised FCF - the FCF-based framework is the more relevant sustainability lens given NZXWT's capitalised-cost/amortisation timing effects.

guidance.management_commentary: Management (Acting CEO Graham Law, ahead of incoming CEO Hishaam Mirza's September 2026 start) characterised H1-2026 as 'solid' despite an 'unsettled environment for global markets and ongoing uncertainty across the New Zealand economy,' citing the US-Iran conflict and a slower NZ economic cycle as headwinds to primary equity issuance. The Board reiterated confidence in the diversified model - Markets, Smart and NZXWT all grew - and singled out KiwiSaver reform, deeper domestic capital pools and AI-enabled productivity as medium-term opportunities. Incoming CEO Mirza has separately signalled an intent to pursue 'greater scale, liquidity and global relevance,' which may presage strategic changes once he starts in September 2026.

bull_case: KiwiSaver is a genuine, government-mandated structural tailwind: a ~$130b pool that could grow several-fold by 2050, with rising default contribution rates locking in flows that Smart and NZXWT both monetise via FUM- and FUA-based fees

The funds and wealth-technology businesses (Smart + NZXWT, ~49% of H1-2026 revenue) are growing revenue at high-teens to mid-20s percentage rates and are far less cyclical than the legacy exchange-trading business, gradually diversifying NZX away from its riskiest, most cyclical segment

High-payout income stock (70-90% of normalised free cash flow) with a long, unbroken dividend history offers a defensible income floor even if capital-markets activity stays subdued, and normalised FCF conversion (~72% of EBITDA in FY2025) is respectable for a capital-light business

Multiple government-driven tailwinds are converging: KiwiSaver contribution increases, PFI/disclosure relief already delivered, and live political discussion of 'asset recycling' (privatising/listing state and council infrastructure) that could materially refill NZX's IPO pipeline if it proceeds

New CEO with an outside, capital-allocation background (ex-NZ Super) and an explicit 'scale, liquidity, global relevance' mandate could catalyse a more assertive growth or capital-allocation strategy after a decade of stagnant listing numbers
bear_case: The exchange's core moat is a licence, not scale - New Zealand's capital pool is roughly a quarter the size of Australia's, and ASX's own trading volume in NZ-linked stocks already exceeds NZX's total cash-market turnover, meaning the 'national monopoly' framing overstates true competitive insulation

Persistent issuer attrition (Restaurant Brands, Marsden Maritime, Vital Limited all delisted within the past 12-14 months) and a chronically weak IPO pipeline directly shrink the highest-margin Markets segment over time, and management itself (via the incoming CEO) concedes NZX has 'struggled to grow the number of listed companies over the past decade'

Fee-rate compression in passive ETF/KiwiSaver management means rising FUM does not translate cleanly into rising margins - Smart's EBITDA margin (excl. project costs) actually fell year-on-year in H1-2026 even as revenue grew ~19%

Recurring 'one-off' integration and restructure costs (FY2024 $1.3m, FY2025 $1.8m, continuing into H1-2026) suggest an organisation in near-permanent restructuring mode rather than one that has finished integrating its recent (QuayStreet) and current (NZXWT/Smart) transformations

Structural governance overhang: NZX is both the listed company and, via NZ RegCo, the regulator of its own market - a conflict-of-interest optic that persists regardless of formal separation, and a CEO transition (permanent CEO starting only mid-September 2026, after a ~4-month vacancy) adds near-term execution uncertainty
